implementation_notes: Filtering is part of Ruby's core collection protocol: `messages.filter { |m| m[:type] == 'price' }`, with `select`/`find_all` as aliases, `reject` for the discard side, and `grep`/`grep_v` when the criterion is a pattern object (grep applies `===`, so a Regexp, Range or Class works without a block). `Enumerator::Lazy#filter` keeps a pipeline lazy over an unbounded feed and `filter_map` merges criterion and transformation when an accepted message is also reshaped. A filter object is warranted only for configured or stateful criteria (a lambda injected into the consumer), never as a structural pattern.
code_sketch:
KEEP = ->(msg) { msg[:headers]['item_type'] == 'widget' }

queue.each do |msg|                 # or: queue.lazy.filter(&KEEP)
  unless KEEP.call(msg)
    dropped += 1                      # or: dead_letter.publish(msg)
    next
  end
  handler.call(msg)
end

# pattern criteria without a block: names.grep(/\Awidget\./)
pitfalls: Eager Enumerable#filter allocates a new Array for the accepted slice; on a hot message loop prefer `lazy` or an explicit `each` with `next`.
`filter` is an alias of `select` that arrived in Ruby 2.6, so a gem supporting older rubies must call select (find_all is the oldest name), not filter.
grep uses `===`: passing a String matches equality only, so a 'nothing matched' surprise usually means the wrong pattern object was used.
